title: The Stoic evening

lines: THE LOOP THAT KEEPS YOU UP.
cards: Lights out. The head hits the pillow, and the replay starts on its own. The thing you said in the meeting.
The text you didn't answer. The way you snapped at your partner over the dishes. Round and round, the loop that keeps people awake.

Seneca had a different way of ending the day. It took a few minutes, it happened on purpose, and it ended with something like a pardon. He borrowed it from an older philosopher, and he described it in his essay On Anger.

teach.b: First, where Seneca got it. The philosopher Sextius, he tells us, would question his own mind at the end of each day, before sleep. Three questions.
What bad habit have you healed today? What fault have you resisted? In what way are you better?

teach.h: PĒ PAREBĒN: WHERE DID I GO WRONG?
teach.b: The Pythagoreans had verses asking something similar each night: where did I go wrong? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone?
Epictetus quotes those lines to his students. In Greek the first question is pē parebēn: where did I step aside? Third, how Seneca does it.
When the lamp is out, and his wife, who knows his habit, has gone quiet, he goes over his whole day, every word and deed, hiding nothing from himself and skipping nothing.
Then an example: in that argument, you spoke too sharply; don't argue with people who can't be taught. And the verdict: see that you don't do it again.
This time, I forgive you. Fourth, why gently matters. The bedtime replay and the Stoic review look alike, but they work in opposite directions.
The replay is a loop: same scene, more anxiety, no ending.
The review is a line: look, learn one thing, forgive, close the file. Sleep after it is especially sweet, Seneca says, because the mind has been praised or warned and knows where it stands.

how: Some Stoic practitioners end the day with a short review modeled on Seneca and Sextius: what went well, where they slipped, how they grew, followed by self-forgiveness.

o: replaying the day's mistakes until sleep finally comes
Seneca's nightly review: three questions, then a pardon
a list of tomorrow's tasks written out before bed

s: Seneca's evening review ends with harsh self-punishment
he tells himself, don't do it again; this time, I forgive you.
Seneca credits the practice to the philosopher Sextius
Epictetus quotes older verses asking each night where you went wrong

games.q: you're reviewing your day and remember snapping at someone. how does Seneca close the matter?
o: replay it until you feel bad enough
note it, resolve not to repeat it, and forgive yourself
games.why: see that you don't do it again, he says; this time, I forgive you.

practice: Run a short evening review now: what habit did you resist today, where did you slip, and in what way were you better, even slightly? Let one honest answer come to each, without arguing for or against yourself.
Then, if it helps, say Seneca's verdict silently: don't do it again; this time, I forgive you.

wordCard.voice: Stoic evening: Seneca's nightly review, three honest questions about the day, and then a gentle pardon so you can sleep. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, the Pythagorean evening verses Epictetus quotes: where did I go wrong?

carryVoice: Your line: three questions. Then the file closes, and the day can go. Sleep well.
